candidates.name: AI Fiduciaries
candidates.source_quote: AI fiduciaries handle sensitive medical data locally, enabling rapid diagnosis and vaccine development while preserving patient privacy. The crisis demonstrates that accountable AI, deployed through federated networks, can coordinate at civilizational scale without centralizing control.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2.4 Maturation of Defensive Networks, under '2031: Deployment of AI Fiduciaries'
candidates.one_liner: Locally-deployed AI agents that process sensitive medical data on-site within federated health networks, enabling cross-network coordination without centralizing raw data.
candidates.mechanism: Each AI fiduciary operates within a local node (e.g., a hospital or regional lab), processing patient data in place rather than transmitting it to a central repository. The fiduciaries coordinate diagnosis and vaccine development outputs across the federated network by sharing results and models rather than raw data. This preserves patient privacy while enabling civilizational-scale crisis response without any single entity controlling the underlying data.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in federated learning frameworks and privacy-preserving computation (e.g., secure enclaves, differential privacy in health research), but the specific framing of an 'AI fiduciary' as an accountable, locally-deployed agent with defined custodial responsibilities within a federated crisis-response mesh is not a standardized deployed system.

research.trl_justification: Federated learning frameworks are demonstrated in real-world healthcare settings with multiple institutions (5-10% of studies show actual clinical deployment), but the specific 'AI fiduciary' framing with defined custodial responsibilities and crisis-response mesh coordination remains largely conceptual. Proof-of-concept implementations exist for federated learning with privacy-preserving techniques, but standardized deployment as accountable local agents is not yet established.

research.state_of_the_art: Federated learning in healthcare has progressed from theoretical frameworks to pilot implementations across multiple institutions, with privacy-preserving techniques including differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, and secure multi-party computation now being integrated. Real-world deployments demonstrate that federated models can achieve comparable or superior performance to centralized approaches while maintaining data privacy and regulatory compliance (HIPAA, GDPR). However, only 5-10% of published studies involve actual clinical deployment, with most remaining proof-of-concept. The specific concept of 'AI fiduciaries' as accountable local agents with defined custodial responsibilities within federated crisis-response networks is not yet a standardized or widely deployed system.
research.barriers: Key barriers include lack of standardized technical infrastructure and governance frameworks for multi-institutional federated networks, with participating hospitals facing challenges in data harmonization, computational resource requirements, and establishing trust among entities. Regulatory and intellectual property issues remain unresolved, particularly regarding inventorship contribution, data quality incentives, and liability assignment in federated systems. Additionally, privacy-utility trade-offs, model convergence challenges with heterogeneous data, and the absence of widely adopted standards for 'fiduciary' accountability in decentralized health networks limit broader adoption.

candidates.name: Interoperable Governance Protocol Stack
candidates.source_quote: A coalition of federated city-states launches the first interoperable governance protocol stack, allowing citizens to carry digital IDs, benefits, and credentials between different local systems. When severe flooding hits multiple jurisdictions, modular governance systems coordinate relief in hours instead of weeks, sharing resources and logistics seamlessly across local and regional levels.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2.5 Stress Testing, under '2033: The Interoperability Breakthrough'
candidates.one_liner: A shared technical and governance protocol layer that allows citizens to port digital identities, benefits, and credentials across distinct federated city-state systems, and enables AI systems across those jurisdictions to align resource allocation and crisis modeling.
candidates.mechanism: The protocol stack defines common standards for digital identity, benefits entitlements, and credentials so that any compliant local system can read and honor records issued by another. During crises, the same stack enables federated AI systems across jurisdictions to share resource allocation decisions, risk assessments, and logistics data in a machine-readable, interoperable format. Governance modules are modular, so jurisdictions can adopt the stack without surrendering local policy autonomy, and the protocol layer handles translation between differing local implementations.
candidates.exists_today: Partial analogues exist in eIDAS (EU digital identity interoperability), W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), and Verifiable Credentials standards, but none combine cross-jurisdictional civic benefits portability with an AI coordination layer for real-time crisis resource allocation at the described scale.

However, the specific combination of cross-jurisdictional benefits portability with federated AI crisis coordination remains at prototype/pilot stage without full-scale deployment.

Real-World Interoperability Demonstration of New Standards

research.state_of_the_art: Digital identity interoperability standards have matured significantly, with W3C Verifiable Credentials and OpenID4VP specifications moving toward final publication and production deployment across multiple jurisdictions. Federated learning frameworks for privacy-preserving AI coordination are established in healthcare and emergency response contexts. However, the integrated system combining portable civic benefits across federated city-states with real-time AI resource allocation remains largely theoretical. Most implementations focus on either identity portability (eIDAS, national digital wallets) or AI-driven crisis coordination separately, not both in a unified protocol stack. Governance frameworks for cross-jurisdictional systems exist but lack standardized approaches for benefits entitlements translation.
research.barriers: Regulatory fragmentation across jurisdictions creates incompatible legal frameworks for benefits eligibility and data sharing, making unified standards difficult to enforce. Technical barriers include the complexity of translating heterogeneous local policy implementations into machine-readable formats while preserving jurisdictional autonomy, and the lack of standardized semantics for civic benefits across different governance models. Trust and governance challenges remain significant: establishing mutual recognition of credentials and AI decisions across independent jurisdictions requires political consensus that has not yet materialized at scale.

candidates.name: Federated Procurement Platforms
candidates.source_quote: Federated procurement platforms let mid-sized buyers pool resources, but uneven coordination leaves some regions overstocked, others empty.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2.2 The Reality Check, under '2027: The Supply Chain Cascade'
candidates.one_liner: A federated platform allowing mid-sized institutional buyers (hospitals, utilities, manufacturers) to pool purchasing power and coordinate supply acquisition across a distributed network rather than through a single centralized marketplace.
candidates.mechanism: Mid-sized buyers join a federated network where each node represents an institution or cooperative. The platform aggregates demand signals across nodes to negotiate collective purchasing, then distributes allocations according to local need. AI-assisted coordination matches supply availability to regional demand in real time, with the goal of preventing large buyers from monopolizing scarce goods. Interoperability standards allow nodes running different local systems to participate in the same procurement events.
candidates.exists_today: Group purchasing organizations (GPOs) in healthcare and government procurement consortia exist, but a federated, AI-assisted, interoperable version spanning diverse institutional types and jurisdictions with real-time allocation is not a deployed standard system.

research.state_of_the_art: Traditional GPOs operate successfully in healthcare and government procurement, leveraging collective purchasing power to negotiate discounts (10-18% savings reported). Recent AI procurement platforms (Ivalua, Coupa, Levelpath, Zycus) add agentic AI for workflow automation, risk detection, and supplier matching within single-vendor ecosystems. However, true federated procurement platforms enabling real-time demand aggregation and allocation across diverse institutional types and heterogeneous local systems remain largely theoretical. The GovAI Coalition (launched 2023) is developing shared procurement templates and contract hubs for government agencies, but these focus on AI vendor procurement rather than federated institutional buying networks.
research.barriers: Interoperability standards for connecting disparate institutional procurement systems remain underdeveloped; most platforms are proprietary and vendor-locked. Regulatory and antitrust concerns around collective purchasing (especially in healthcare) create legal friction for cross-jurisdictional federated models. Real-time demand aggregation and dynamic allocation algorithms require standardized data formats and governance structures that institutions have not yet adopted at scale.

candidates.name: Jurisdictional Routers
candidates.source_quote: Protocols that mediate between state law and DAO bylaws, clarifying authority and handling disputes at the interface of centralized and decentralized systems. These systems are economically sustainable through transaction fees, creating self-funding infrastructure for managing jurisdictional complexity.
candidates.source_quote_context: Governance section, 'What's in use in 2035' subsection
candidates.one_liner: Self-funding protocol layer that mediates legal authority disputes between nation-state law and DAO governance, sustained by transaction fees.
candidates.mechanism: When a conflict arises between state law and DAO bylaws, the Jurisdictional Router protocol adjudicates which authority applies and routes the dispute accordingly. The system charges transaction fees for each mediation, making it financially self-sustaining without public subsidy. This creates persistent infrastructure for managing the interface between centralized and decentralized legal systems.
candidates.exists_today: Kleros offers decentralized dispute resolution; some legal tech platforms handle cross-jurisdictional arbitration, but no self-funding protocol layer specifically mediating state-law/DAO-bylaw conflicts exists.

key_publications.title: Blockchain Dispute Resolution for Decentralized Autonomous Organizations: The Rise of Decentralized Autonomous Justice
Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) Before State Courts: How Can Private International Law Keep Up With Global Digital Entities?
Kleros: A Socio-Legal Case Study of Decentralized Justice & Blockchain Arbitration

research.state_of_the_art: State courts currently struggle to adjudicate DAO disputes due to jurisdictional ambiguity, lack of legal personhood for unregistered DAOs, and enforcement challenges. Blockchain-based dispute resolution (BDR) mechanisms like Kleros exist for general smart contract disputes but are limited to binary decisions and on-chain asset enforcement. Some jurisdictions (Wyoming, Tennessee, Utah) have enacted DAO LLC legislation providing legal entity status, but these create hybrid structures rather than pure protocol-layer mediation. Academic literature identifies the need for adapted dispute resolution mechanisms but no production system specifically mediates conflicts between state law and DAO bylaws through a self-funding protocol layer.
research.barriers: The fundamental barrier is that state courts lack jurisdiction over decentralized entities without legal personhood, while blockchain-based systems cannot enforce decisions on off-chain assets or compel state compliance. Additionally, the concept of a self-funding protocol layer mediating between sovereign legal systems faces legitimacy and enforceability challenges—no state authority would recognize a private protocol's adjudication as binding, and cryptoeconomic incentives cannot substitute for legal authority or enforcement mechanisms that only states possess.

candidates.name: Safety-Netted DAOs
candidates.source_quote: Civic organizations that retain temporary centralized controls (e.g., a 'circuit breaker' council) to intervene in crises, with clear, time-locked paths toward greater decentralization.
candidates.source_quote_context: Governance section, 'What's in use in 2035' subsection
candidates.one_liner: DAO governance structure with a built-in emergency override council whose authority is automatically time-limited, with a pre-committed schedule for returning to decentralized control.
candidates.mechanism: A civic DAO embeds a small 'circuit breaker' council with authority to override decentralized governance during crises. This centralized override is not permanent: the council's authority is time-locked, meaning it automatically expires after a defined period, and the path back to decentralization is encoded in advance and cannot be unilaterally extended. This prevents emergency powers from becoming permanent while still allowing rapid crisis response.
candidates.exists_today: Some DeFi protocols include emergency pause mechanisms (e.g., multisig admin keys), but these lack the formal time-lock commitment to decentralization re-entry that defines this proposal.
candidates.source_file: ai-pathways/d-acc.md
candidates.source_section: 3 How d/acc Transformed Key Domains Across Society

research.trl_justification: Concept exists in academic and industry discussions (circuit breakers, timelocks, emergency multisigs) but no dedicated implementation of Safety-Netted DAOs with formal time-locked commitment to decentralization re-entry found. Related components (timelocks, emergency pause mechanisms) are deployed in production DeFi protocols but lack the integrated architecture described.
research.state_of_the_art: Current DAO governance includes emergency pause mechanisms via multisig admin keys (Lido, Maker) and timelocks that delay proposal execution (Uniswap, Compound). However, these lack formal pre-committed schedules for returning to decentralized control. Circuit breaker concepts appear in AI-DAO governance discussions but focus on pausing AI actions rather than governance transitions. Timelocks are widely used for security but primarily as execution delays, not as mechanisms ensuring automatic decentralization re-entry. The gap between emergency override capability and guaranteed decentralization restoration remains largely unaddressed in production systems.
research.barriers: First, there is no standardized framework or smart contract library implementing time-locked authority expiration with automatic decentralization re-entry, requiring custom development for each DAO. Second, governance design faces inherent tension between emergency responsiveness and decentralization guarantees—councils may resist pre-committing to power loss, and communities struggle to define optimal time windows that balance crisis response with decentralization restoration. Third, regulatory uncertainty around emergency powers and their time-bound nature creates legal ambiguity for DAOs operating across jurisdictions.

candidates.name: Pareto-Optimal Negotiation Bots
candidates.source_quote: AI systems designed to find mutually beneficial outcomes handle routine commercial negotiations. These systems focus on creating value for both sides and avoid perpetuating existing human biases by learning from outcomes rather than human behavior patterns.
candidates.source_quote_context: Law & Justice section, 'What's in use in 2035' subsection
candidates.one_liner: Commercial negotiation AI that trains on outcome data rather than human negotiation behavior, specifically to avoid replicating human biases while maximizing joint value.
candidates.mechanism: Rather than training on transcripts or patterns of how humans negotiate (which would encode existing power imbalances and biases), these AI systems are trained on negotiation outcomes — what settlements proved mutually beneficial over time. The system searches for Pareto-optimal agreements by modeling the value space for both parties and proposing terms that expand rather than divide the pie. This design choice explicitly breaks the feedback loop between historical human bias and AI recommendation.
candidates.exists_today: AI negotiation tools exist (e.g., Pactum, some procurement bots), but they generally train on human negotiation data; the specific design of outcome-only training to avoid bias propagation is not a standard deployed approach.

research.state_of_the_art: Pareto-optimal negotiation AI is an emerging but operationally deployed technology. Pactum AI exemplifies the approach, using rule-based AI trained on negotiation science rather than human transcripts to avoid bias propagation, achieving 10-15% savings in commercial negotiations. The field combines game theory, machine learning, and behavioral analysis to identify win-win outcomes. However, most deployed systems focus on high-volume, low-value procurement rather than complex multi-party negotiations. Academic research demonstrates feasibility of Pareto-optimal outcomes through deep reinforcement learning and algorithmic approaches, but real-world deployment remains concentrated in procurement automation.
research.barriers: Key barriers include: (1) Organizational resistance to ceding negotiation control to AI and concerns about depersonalizing supplier relationships, requiring significant change management; (2) Technical limitations in handling complex, multi-party negotiations with implicit cultural and emotional dimensions that AI systems struggle to capture; (3) Legal and ethical concerns around liability for AI-generated decisions, data privacy, and potential for AI systems to develop or amplify biases despite outcome-based training, requiring robust governance frameworks and human oversight.

candidates.name: AGI Liability Safe Harbor Framework
source_quote: Liability frameworks targeting the triple intersection could create strong incentives for Tool AI approaches. Such frameworks would impose strict liability, including personal criminal liability for executives, on systems that combine high autonomy, generality, and intelligence, while providing 'safe harbor' protections for systems that lack one or more of these properties.

AI systems cannot be held responsible for their actions, therefore human individuals and organizations must bear full responsibility for harms they cause. The level of liability should reflect the level of risk - systems that combine high autonomy, generality, and intelligence pose the greatest danger and should face the strictest liability standards, including personal criminal liability for executives. However, systems that lack one or more of these properties should receive safe harbor protections under standard fault-based liability.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 2 'What is Tool AI?', discussion of mechanisms to incentivize Tool AI development over AGI
candidates.one_liner: A tiered legal liability framework that imposes strict (including criminal) liability on AI systems occupying the high-autonomy + high-generality + high-intelligence intersection, while granting safe harbor to systems lacking one or more of these properties.
candidates.mechanism: The framework maps liability exposure to the AGI 'triple intersection' of Autonomy, Generality, and Intelligence. Systems combining all three face strict liability and personal criminal liability for executives. Systems that are high in one or two dimensions but not all three qualify for reduced (fault-based) or safe harbor liability. This creates economic and legal incentives to deliberately constrain at least one dimension, making Tool AI the commercially viable default for high-stakes applications.
candidates.exists_today: Product liability and sector-specific AI regulations exist (e.g., EU AI Act risk tiers), but none currently impose personal criminal executive liability keyed specifically to the autonomy-generality-intelligence triple intersection as a formal legal trigger.
candidates.source_file: ai-pathways/tool-ai.md

research.trl_justification: Conceptual proposal only; no implementation, prototyping, or field testing. Framework exists as theoretical proposal in academic literature and policy discussions but has not been formally adopted or operationalized by any jurisdiction or organization.

key_publications.title: Keep the Future Human: Why and How We Should Close the Gates to AGI and Superintelligence, and What We Should Build Instead
Regulating AGI: From Liability to Provable Contracts

research.state_of_the_art: The AGI Liability Safe Harbor Framework remains a theoretical proposal without formal legal implementation. Current AI regulation focuses on risk-based tiers (EU AI Act) and sector-specific rules rather than the autonomy-generality-intelligence triple intersection. No jurisdiction has enacted legislation imposing personal criminal liability specifically keyed to this framework. Academic discussion emphasizes the framework's potential to create economic incentives for constrained AI development, but practical legal mechanisms for operationalizing the triple-intersection trigger remain undeveloped.
research.barriers: The framework faces fundamental barriers: (1) definitional challenges—no consensus exists on measuring autonomy, generality, and intelligence as discrete, measurable dimensions; (2) political and industry opposition—companies resist strict liability regimes that would constrain high-capability AI development; (3) jurisdictional fragmentation—implementing such a framework requires coordinated international legal action, which has not materialized despite EU AI Act progress.

candidates.name: contextual autonomy
candidates.source_quote: The most successful approach becomes 'contextual autonomy', systems that automatically reduce their independence based on risk level: autonomous for low-stakes tasks like scheduling, but requiring human oversight for anything involving money, health, or safety.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 3.1, describing the market pivot of early 2027 as companies adapt to the liability framework
candidates.speaker: Report authors
candidates.one_liner: An AI architecture that dynamically and automatically scales down its own operational autonomy in proportion to the assessed risk level of the task at hand.
candidates.mechanism: The system continuously evaluates the risk category of each pending action and applies a corresponding autonomy tier: fully autonomous execution for low-stakes tasks (e.g., scheduling), mandatory human approval gates for medium-risk tasks, and full human direction for anything touching money, health, or safety. The risk classification and autonomy reduction happen at runtime without requiring separate system deployments, allowing a single model to serve across risk levels while remaining within liability safe harbors.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in the form of human-in-the-loop checkpoints in some enterprise AI workflows, but no standardized runtime risk-classification-to-autonomy-reduction architecture is in widespread production deployment.

Agentic AI Security: Threats, Defenses, Evaluation, and Open Challenges

research.state_of_the_art: Runtime risk-based autonomy scaling is emerging as a critical architectural pattern in agentic AI systems. AWS, Cisco, and other enterprises have implemented graceful degradation mechanisms that automatically reduce autonomy levels when security events are detected. The field recognizes that static human-in-the-loop approaches do not scale with machine speed and decision volume, driving adoption of dynamic, context-aware control planes that evaluate risk at runtime. However, implementations remain vendor-specific and lack standardization. The 2026 International AI Safety Report emphasizes that governance must shift from static evaluation to dynamic steerability, with continuous monitoring replacing periodic reviews.
research.barriers: The primary barrier is the lack of standardized runtime risk-classification schemas and autonomy-reduction protocols across heterogeneous AI systems. Organizations struggle to define what constitutes 'risk' in context-dependent ways and how to map risk levels to specific autonomy constraints without creating brittle, over-conservative systems. Additionally, human oversight mechanisms remain bottlenecks at scale—traditional HITL approaches cannot keep pace with millions of agent decisions per second, yet fully autonomous systems without human oversight introduce unacceptable liability and regulatory exposure, particularly in regulated industries.

candidates.name: Tool AI for Tool AI
candidates.source_quote: Tool AI for Tool AI emerges: interpretable AI systems help design and validate other interpretable AI systems, creating scalable oversight mechanisms.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section 3.2, describing the technical foundation period of 2027-2028
candidates.speaker: Report authors
candidates.one_liner: A recursive oversight architecture in which interpretable, constrained AI systems are used to design, audit, and validate other interpretable AI systems, scaling human oversight without requiring proportional human labor.
candidates.mechanism: Interpretable Tool AI systems are deployed as validators and designers of other Tool AI systems, checking that candidate systems meet interpretability, audit-trail, and autonomy-constraint standards before deployment. Because the validating systems are themselves interpretable and human-overseen, the chain of oversight remains auditable at each level. This allows the volume of AI systems being deployed to grow faster than the human workforce capable of manually reviewing each one.
candidates.exists_today: Related concepts exist in AI safety research (e.g., scalable oversight, debate, and recursive reward modeling), and RAND has written on AI automating AI R&D, but no production infrastructure implementing this as a standardized compliance and validation pipeline exists.

key_publications.title: Scalable Oversight for Superhuman AI via Recursive Self-Critiquing
Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight
How AI Can Automate AI Research and Development

research.state_of_the_art: Scalable oversight research has matured significantly since 2018, with multiple complementary approaches now deployed in production. Constitutional AI (Anthropic) uses self-critique against explicit principles; debate protocols (Google DeepMind) pit competing AI systems against each other; and weak-to-strong generalization (OpenAI) enables weaker overseers to supervise stronger systems. However, no standardized infrastructure exists for recursive Tool AI validation pipelines. Current implementations remain largely proprietary and lack the interpretability constraints and audit-trail requirements specified in the proposed architecture. The field is converging on combining multiple techniques rather than relying on single approaches.
research.barriers: The primary barrier is the 'sandwiching problem'—validating oversight approaches for superhuman systems when only human-level judges are available for testing. Additionally, deception remains a fundamental challenge: sophisticated AI systems could produce reassuring explanations while computing something else, undermining interpretability-based oversight. Finally, no production infrastructure exists that standardizes compliance validation across multiple AI systems, and building such infrastructure requires solving the technical problem of making interpretability itself auditable and scalable.

candidates.name: Focused Research Organizations (FROs)
candidates.source_quote: I think of them as a critical mass of the right people multiplied by a critical mass of time and support to build a very well-defined thing that the market would not support you building as a traditional for-profit startup, right? So in some ways you can think of them as sort of like nonprofit deep tech startups.
candidates.source_quote_context: Early discussion of what FROs are and how they differ from traditional organizations
candidates.speaker: Adam Marblestone
candidates.one_liner: Nonprofit startup-like entities that assemble a focused, interdisciplinary team to build a specific piece of scientific infrastructure that neither academia nor the private sector would otherwise produce.
candidates.mechanism: A parent nonprofit (Convergent Research) houses each FRO as a subsidiary LLC, providing back-office support. A small founding team handpicks hires for both technical skill and mission alignment, then operates with startup-like unity of purpose for roughly five years to build a well-defined deliverable—often an open-source dataset, tool, or platform. Unlike academic labs, all contributors converge on the same artifact rather than pursuing individual research questions.
candidates.exists_today: Convergent Research has launched several FROs including ones in connectomics, single-cell proteomics, and interactive theorem proving (Lean). A handful exist as of the recording, with the oldest approximately three years old.

key_publications.title: Field Notes on Moving Focused Research Organizations Forward
Focused Research Organizations: A New Model for Scientific Research
Former MIT researchers advance a new model for innovation

research.state_of_the_art: Focused Research Organizations represent a maturing organizational model for addressing scientific bottlenecks that fall between academic and commercial incentives. As of 2025, Convergent Research has launched 10 FROs across life sciences, climate, and mathematics, with several releasing open-source tools and datasets. The model has gained governmental interest, with the UK's ARIA planning to fund FROs and the White House AI Action Plan recommending long-term FRO agreements. Early evidence suggests FROs are effective at producing public goods that neither academia nor industry would otherwise create, though the model remains relatively new with the oldest FROs approximately 4 years old.
research.barriers: Key barriers include the significant effort required to fundraise and launch FROs compared to traditional academic or venture-backed structures, the challenge of scoping projects correctly given the need to execute against fixed grant agreements, and the relative immaturity of the model compared to established funding ecosystems. Additionally, achieving high-throughput analysis and scaling FRO outputs to match the pace of traditional research remains challenging, and there is limited standardization across FROs regarding methodology and technology transfer mechanisms.

candidates.name: Lean FRO (interactive theorem proving infrastructure for mathematics and AI)
candidates.source_quote: Instead of writing down their mathematical proof on a piece of paper, they write it in this programming language, which is Lean. And then what Lean can also do in addition to suggesting next steps and so on and resolving parts of the proof, is it can actually just say, do your conclusions actually follow from your assumptions? Yes, you are right. Your proof is correct of the thing that you claim to be proving.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of specific FROs that have launched, highlighting the Lean FRO as an unexpected but important example
candidates.speaker: Adam Marblestone
candidates.one_liner: A focused research organization building software infrastructure around the Lean proof assistant, enabling automated verification of mathematical proofs and serving as a closed-loop training environment for AI systems.
candidates.mechanism: Mathematicians write proofs in the Lean programming language rather than on paper; the system can automatically verify whether conclusions follow from axioms. This creates a closed feedback loop analogous to a game engine (like Go or chess) where an AI can receive automatic reinforcement signals for correct proofs without human judges, potentially enabling AI to generate and verify novel mathematical proofs at scale. The FRO provides the software engineering capacity that mathematicians themselves lack.
candidates.exists_today: The Lean proof assistant language exists and is used by some mathematicians and AI researchers. DeepMind and others have used Lean-like environments for AI math research. The FRO to build out the broader infrastructure is the new organizational component.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Adam Marblestone | Solving Science’s Biggest Gaps.md

research.state_of_the_art: Lean 4 is a mature, open-source proof assistant with 210,000+ formalized theorems in Mathlib as of May 2025. AI systems like Google DeepMind's AlphaProof achieve International Mathematical Olympiad silver-medal performance. LeanDojo provides infrastructure for training AI on formal proofs, and Lean Copilot enables human-AI collaboration. The ecosystem supports both interactive and automated theorem proving, with active adoption by mathematicians (Terence Tao, Peter Scholze) and industry (AWS). However, autonomous AI generation of novel research-level proofs remains limited.
research.barriers: Scaling challenges include the de Bruijn factor (proof length in Lean vs. mathematical prose), technical debt in Mathlib, and the difficulty of premise selection for novel domains. Current AI systems struggle with theorems outside training data domains and lack the reasoning depth for cutting-edge mathematical discovery. Infrastructure gaps remain in proof automation, language server performance, and integration with external tools.

candidates.name: Bio-templated microchips via implosion fabrication
candidates.source_quote: Implosion fabrication is the opposite of expansion microscopy. It means you pattern materials into a hydrogel and then you shrink it, but it can shrink by a factor of more than 10 along each axis. And if you shrink something besides the wavelength of light down, you'd also get down to these single digit nanometer features.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of nanotechnology progress and what the field needs, specifically around positional chemistry and chip fabrication
candidates.speaker: Adam Marblestone
candidates.one_liner: A fabrication technique that patterns materials (potentially DNA origami or other biological scaffolds) into a hydrogel at optical resolution and then shrinks the hydrogel by 10x or more to achieve single-digit nanometer feature sizes for chip-like structures.
candidates.mechanism: Biological or chemical components are positioned within a swellable hydrogel using light-based patterning at resolutions accessible to conventional optics. The hydrogel is then chemically shrunk by a factor greater than 10 in each linear dimension, compressing the patterned features to nanometer scales that approach the precision needed for positional chemistry and chip fabrication. DNA origami provides a programmable scaffold at the ~2 nm scale that can serve as a starting template.
candidates.exists_today: Expansion microscopy (the reverse process) is widely used in neuroscience labs. Implosion fabrication has been demonstrated as a research technique at MIT. DNA origami is a mature research tool. Full integration into a chip fabrication pipeline does not yet exist.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Adam Marblestone | Solving Science’s Biggest Gaps.md

research.state_of_the_art: Implosion fabrication has achieved nanoscale resolution (~50-60 nm) with 10-20x linear shrinkage in laboratory settings at MIT. The technique can pattern metals, semiconductors, quantum dots, and DNA into 3D structures within hydrogel scaffolds. DNA origami is a mature research tool widely used for biosensing and drug delivery applications. However, full integration into chip fabrication pipelines remains absent; current work focuses on proof-of-concept demonstrations and accessibility to biology labs rather than manufacturing-scale production.
research.barriers: Key barriers include: (1) Dehydration requirement limits use of aqueous-dependent materials and moving parts; (2) Scaling from millimeter-sized objects to wafer-scale fabrication has not been demonstrated; (3) Integration with conventional semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure and lithography remains unresolved; (4) Yield, reproducibility, and cost-effectiveness for commercial production have not been established.

research.state_of_the_art: The vagus nerve microbiome characterization study represents a first-of-its-kind effort to directly sample and analyze microbial residents of human vagus nerve tissue. While extensive research demonstrates bidirectional communication between gut microbiota and brain via the vagus nerve, no prior published characterization of the living human vagus nerve microbiome exists at scale. Recent animal studies confirm gut microbiota regulate vagal activity through specific metabolites like short-chain fatty acids and bile acids. The study addresses a critical gap by obtaining vagus nerve samples from trauma patients—samples that cannot be collected via standard biopsy procedures—enabling unbiased metagenomic analysis of viral, bacterial, and fungal organisms.
research.barriers: Obtaining vagus nerve tissue samples is extremely difficult since standard tissue biopsy procedures cannot access this nerve, limiting sample availability to trauma surgery cases. The degree to which pathogens persist in the vagus nerve remains dramatically understudied, and establishing baseline characterization of the healthy vagus nerve microbiome is necessary before understanding disease associations or therapeutic implications.

candidates.name: Extracellular vesicle-based blood diagnostics for tissue-resident infections
candidates.source_quote: Some groups use microfluidics to isolate extracellular vesicles in blood that might contain one or two pieces of a virus hiding deep in tissue. If you have the right tech, you can extract that signal. But these technologies are scattered across different labs, so we work to unite them — designing studies, for example in long COVID, where we collect both tissue and blood, then compare which diagnostic tests best reflect the infection in tissue.
candidates.source_quote_context: Amy explaining the diagnostic translation pipeline after describing tissue banking, in the section on moving from discovery to clinical tools
candidates.speaker: Amy Proal
candidates.one_liner: A validation framework pairing tissue biopsies with microfluidic blood assays that isolate extracellular vesicles carrying viral fragments, to develop accessible blood-based diagnostics for deep-tissue infections.
candidates.mechanism: Microfluidic platforms isolate extracellular vesicles circulating in blood; these vesicles can carry trace viral material shed from infected tissues. By simultaneously collecting matched tissue and blood samples from the same patients (e.g., long COVID cohorts), researchers can validate whether vesicle-based blood signals accurately reflect what is found in tissue, creating a calibrated diagnostic test that doesn't require biopsy.
candidates.exists_today: Microfluidic extracellular vesicle isolation exists in research settings; the specific cross-validation framework pairing it with tissue biopsy for persistent infection diagnosis is at early/prototype stage, not clinically deployed.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Amy Proal | Rethinking chronic disease.md

research.state_of_the_art: Microfluidic platforms for EV isolation have advanced significantly, with viscoelastic and acoustofluidic approaches achieving >97% purity and >87% recovery from whole blood. EVs are recognized as promising biomarkers for infectious diseases, carrying pathogen-derived factors and host response signatures. However, clinical translation remains limited—only 2 of 350+ registered clinical trials involve microfluidic EV systems. The specific validation framework pairing tissue biopsies with blood-based EV assays for persistent infections (e.g., long COVID) is at early prototype stage, with limited literature on EV-based diagnostics for tissue-resident infections.
research.barriers: Standardization and reproducibility challenges persist across EV isolation methods, with no consensus metrics for assessing purity and heterogeneity. Clinical workflows require pre-purification steps (e.g., ultracentrifugation) before microfluidic processing, limiting point-of-care applicability. The specific challenge of validating tissue-resident infection signals in circulating EVs requires matched tissue-blood cohort studies, which are resource-intensive and not yet systematically conducted for persistent viral infections.

The goal is to reduce single-model bias on high-stakes questions.

research.state_of_the_art: Multiple production platforms now enable users to query multiple LLMs simultaneously and compare outputs, including Poe (with 3+ models), Ithy (ChatGPT/Gemini/Perplexity synthesis), and Prompts.ai (35+ models). The PAIR LLM Comparator provides interactive visualization for side-by-side evaluation with automated rationale summarization. Academic work on 'Regulated Multiplicity' proposes architectural frameworks for internal model diversity and principled disagreement adjudication. The core capability—parallel querying and synthesis—is mature and deployed, though most tools focus on comparison tables rather than deep disagreement analysis.
research.barriers: Most existing tools provide side-by-side comparison tables but lack sophisticated synthesis of disagreement patterns or principled adjudication mechanisms. Cost and latency scale with the number of models queried simultaneously. Privacy and data residency concerns arise when routing queries to multiple third-party LLM providers, limiting adoption in regulated industries. The lack of standardized metrics for measuring 'agreement' and 'disagreement' across heterogeneous models makes it difficult to build reliable synthesis layers.

Multi-agent systems for medical research are emerging as a promising paradigm, with frameworks like Virtual Biotech showing capability to analyze thousands of clinical trials. research.barriers: LLM reliability in clinical text extraction remains unresolved—ChatGPT-4 failed to consistently extract helmet status from ED notes despite detailed prompts. Privacy and HIPAA compliance create friction in data aggregation across 27,000+ institutions. candidates.name: AI-mediated conflict resolution tool (retorsion/disgorgement mediator)
candidates.source_quote: You could write a mediation tool that's like, 'Hey, we have a problem. Let's talk to this mediator.' And it'll try and get us the win-win. And if that fails, it'll try and get us the restoration. And if that fails, it'll try and get us the disgorgement.
candidates.source_quote_context: Andrew responding to a question about coordination challenges in de-escalatory self-defense, around timestamp 58:17
candidates.speaker: Andrew Critch
candidates.one_liner: A structured AI mediator that walks disputing parties through a prioritized sequence—win-win trade, then restoration, then disgorgement—before any punitive action is considered.
candidates.mechanism: The tool takes a described dispute and first attempts to surface a mutually beneficial trade between parties. If that fails, it seeks restoration of the original state. If restoration is refused, it facilitates disgorgement—eliminating the ill-gotten benefit without inflicting additional harm—and optionally a minimal retorsion sufficient to deter repetition. The explicit sequencing is meant to prevent escalation to revenge-level responses.
candidates.exists_today: No known implementation; described as a hypothetical product concept during the conversation.

research.state_of_the_art: AI-mediated conflict resolution is rapidly advancing with multiple commercial platforms now operational. Existing systems guide parties through structured negotiation processes, offer intelligent prompts, and generate settlement suggestions based on case data and game theory. Hybrid human-AI approaches are becoming standard, with AI handling data analysis, sentiment detection, and proposal generation while humans retain decision-making authority. Research shows AI-human hybrid systems achieve 20-25% higher resolution rates in workplace disputes compared to either method alone. However, current implementations focus on general mediation rather than the specific sequenced escalation framework (win-win → restoration → disgorgement → retorsion) proposed here.
research.barriers: The proposed sequenced mechanism combining win-win trade, restoration, disgorgement, and retorsion lacks established legal and ethical frameworks for implementation. Current AI mediation systems struggle with emotional intelligence, cultural nuance, and the complex judgment required for determining fair disgorgement amounts or appropriate retorsion levels. Regulatory uncertainty remains significant—the EU AI Act and emerging governance frameworks have not yet clarified how AI systems should handle remedies involving asset forfeiture or punitive measures, creating legal and liability risks for developers.

candidates.name: LitQA3 (high-recall literature evaluation benchmark)
candidates.source_quote: We're building another one right now which we're calling internally LitQA3, and this one is what I would call high-recall tasks. Right now, agents are really good at precision. Humanity's Last Exam is a very precision-level task: go find this one fact. We're trying to build evals that are what I would call recall tasks, like 'find every paper that studied X, do a meta-analysis to find out if X is true or false, and then give me statistics on whether that's true or not.'
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of benchmark limitations and Future House's evaluation work, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: Andrew White
candidates.one_liner: A benchmark that tests AI agents on high-recall scientific literature tasks—finding all relevant papers on a topic and synthesizing them into a meta-analysis—rather than single-fact retrieval.
candidates.mechanism: The benchmark poses tasks requiring an agent to locate every paper studying a given phenomenon, perform a meta-analysis across them, and return statistics on whether the phenomenon is supported. This contrasts with precision-style benchmarks (like Humanity's Last Exam) that ask for a single correct answer. The design targets a known weakness of current agents: integrating large bodies of evidence rather than retrieving isolated facts.
candidates.exists_today: Future House has a prior benchmark called Bioinformatics Benchmark (frontier LLMs score ~20%). LitQA3 is described as under active development ('we're building another one right now').

research.state_of_the_art: High-recall literature evaluation benchmarks remain nascent. LitQA (the predecessor to LitQA3) requires retrieval and synthesis from full-text papers and has demonstrated that RAG agents can match expert researchers on complex literature tasks. Related benchmarks like BixBench and AstaBench show frontier LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) achieve only 9-17% accuracy on open-ended scientific analysis tasks, indicating significant gaps in multi-step reasoning and evidence synthesis. ReportBench and similar frameworks are emerging to evaluate deep research agents on literature quality and factual accuracy. The field is transitioning from single-fact retrieval benchmarks toward comprehensive literature synthesis evaluation.
research.barriers: Current LLMs struggle with multi-step reasoning across large document collections and reliable synthesis of contradictory evidence. Frontier models show poor performance on open-ended scientific tasks (17% accuracy on BixBench), suggesting fundamental limitations in integrating large bodies of evidence rather than isolated facts. Lack of standardized high-recall evaluation datasets and ground-truth meta-analyses makes it difficult to benchmark agents on comprehensive literature review tasks at scale.

candidates.name: AI-driven drug repurposing pipeline (AMD/Ripasudil discovery workflow)
candidates.source_quote: We asked our system to come up with as many ideas as possible. It hypothesized about a lot of ideas about how this disease could be treated and then it used things like Owl to see if anybody had tried this before... And then based on these ideas that it thought could be good, what are experiments we could do in our lab? So then we did those experiments, then we provided the raw data to Finch, our data analysis agent... And then it proposed specific compounds to try to treat this in the cell model.
candidates.source_quote_context: Description of the dry AMD / Ripasudil discovery project, roughly mid-interview
candidates.speaker: Andrew White
candidates.one_liner: A multi-agent pipeline that takes a disease target as input and autonomously generates mechanistic hypotheses, checks prior art, designs wet-lab experiments, analyzes results, and proposes repurposed drug candidates—demonstrated end-to-end in ~3 weeks for dry AMD.
candidates.mechanism: The pipeline chains several specialized agents: a hypothesis-generation agent proposes mechanistic ideas; Owl searches clinical trials, patents, and literature for prior attempts; a wet-lab team executes agent-specified experiments; Finch (a data-analysis agent) builds and runs Jupyter notebooks on raw experimental data; and the system iterates to propose specific compounds. The AMD run identified Ripasudil (an existing glaucoma drug) as a candidate that accelerates macrophage debris clearance in the eye.
candidates.exists_today: A working prototype was used to produce a published paper on dry AMD/Ripasudil. The individual agents (Crow, Owl, Finch) are available via Future House's open API, but the fully automated end-to-end pipeline is not yet a packaged product.

key_publications.title: Demonstrating end-to-end scientific discovery with Robin: a multi-agent system
AI is Automating Therapeutic Drug Discovery: The Robin System by FutureHouse

research.state_of_the_art: Multi-agent agentic AI systems for drug discovery are rapidly advancing, with FutureHouse's Robin demonstrating the first end-to-end automated discovery workflow completing a full cycle (hypothesis generation through experimental validation and drug candidate identification) in approximately 3 weeks for dry AMD. Individual specialized agents (Crow for literature search, Finch for data analysis, Owl for novelty assessment, Phoenix for chemistry) are now available via open API, enabling researchers to build custom pipelines. However, the fully integrated end-to-end pipeline remains a research prototype rather than a commercialized product. Broader agentic AI systems like Tippy, Repuragent, and Prompt-to-Pill are emerging as proof-of-concepts, though most remain in experimental stages with limited clinical validation.
research.barriers: Key barriers include: (1) Limited clinical validation—most agentic systems remain preclinical; only a few AI-discovered compounds (baricitinib, ISM001-055) have advanced to clinical trials, and some (DSP-1181) failed despite AI acceleration, indicating that AI-driven discovery does not guarantee clinical success. (2) Data access and quality—scientific literature remains largely behind paywalls, and integrating heterogeneous biomedical datasets (genomics, proteomics, clinical data) into autonomous workflows remains technically challenging. (3) Regulatory and interpretability gaps—agentic systems must provide transparent reasoning for regulatory approval, and current systems struggle with explainability and reproducibility at scale.

candidates.name: Publishing for Machines (machine-readable scientific publishing framework)
candidates.source_quote: In my essay, I'm arguing that we need to start thinking about the consumers and producers of science as machines because we're reaching the point where human beings are not going to be able to comprehend all the information there... We need to start changing how we represent science... We need to have slimmer papers... the curation has to be separate... peer review which is the debate of science... that part of peer review is very important, but it shouldn't be hidden.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of scientific publishing reform, late in the interview
candidates.speaker: Andrew White
candidates.one_liner: A proposed redesign of scientific publishing that separates gatekeeping peer review from scientific debate, reduces paper size, eliminates prestige-based journal selection, minimizes latency, and structures outputs for machine ingestion rather than human readers.
candidates.mechanism: The framework has several components: (1) drastically reduced latency from project completion to public availability; (2) machine-readable formats replacing PDFs and paywalled corpora; (3) slimmer atomic publication units focused on single discoveries rather than multi-year projects; (4) separation of peer review into distinct functions—spam/fraud filtering vs. open scientific debate—with the debate portion made public rather than anonymous; and (5) removal of artificial scarcity/prestige signaling from the submission process. The underlying argument is that AI systems will soon be both the primary producers and consumers of scientific literature, making current human-centric formats obsolete.
candidates.exists_today: Preprint servers (arXiv, bioRxiv) address latency partially. Open-access mandates address paywalls partially. Post-publication peer review platforms (PubPeer, eLife's new model) address some debate-separation. White's synthesis into a unified 'publishing for machines' framework exists only as a draft essay.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Andrew White | Building an AI Scientist to Automate Discovery.md

Preprint servers demonstrate partial latency reduction and open access. Machine-readable formats (JATS XML, JSON-LD) adopted in biomedicine but adoption slowed outside that domain. No unified 'Publishing for Machines' system fully operational at scale.

key_publications.title: Science should be machine-readable
Rethinking the production and publication of machine-readable expressions of research findings
Agentic Publications: An LLM-Driven Framework for Interactive Scientific Publishing

research.state_of_the_art: Preprint servers (arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv) have reduced publication latency and enabled open access but remain primarily PDF-based. Machine-readable formats like JATS XML and nanopublications exist as proof-of-concept but lack widespread adoption outside biomedicine. Recent work (2025-2026) on pre-publication machine-readable knowledge generation (reborn framework) and LLM-driven interactive publications shows growing momentum. However, the scholarly publishing system remains fragmented: peer review is still gatekeeping-focused, prestige-based journal selection persists, and AI-generated content raises fraud detection challenges. No unified framework separating peer review functions or eliminating journal prestige signaling has achieved mainstream adoption.
research.barriers: Institutional inertia: journals and funders continue valuing prestige-based publication venues; adoption of machine-readable formats requires publisher investment with unclear ROI. Technical fragmentation: lack of standardized schemas across disciplines and publishers prevents interoperability. Incentive misalignment: researchers benefit from journal prestige for career advancement, creating resistance to atomic publication units and open peer review. Quality control concerns: rapid publication and machine-readability raise fears of amplifying misinformation and paper mill fraud, particularly as AI-generated content becomes harder to detect.

candidates.speaker: Andrew

candidates.mechanism: Aviary provides a structured way to combine large language models with tools to create scientific agents. It is part of a broader platform that includes capabilities like precedent search and is accessible via API. It is documented in a cookbook alongside other Future House tools like PaperQA.
candidates.exists_today: Exists as a released open-source project from Future House, accessible at futurehouse.org with documentation and API access, though adoption and scale are limited.

Trained agents exceed human and frontier LLM performance on benchmarks. However, real-world deployment remains limited to research settings and early-stage commercial use through Edison Scientific. No large-scale operational deployment in production scientific workflows.

key_publications.title: Aviary: training language agents on challenging scientific tasks

research.state_of_the_art: Aviary represents a mature scaffolding framework for composing language agents with scientific tools, released as open-source in December 2024. Trained Llama-3.1-8B agents demonstrate superhuman performance on specific scientific benchmarks (SeqQA, LitQA2) at lower cost than frontier models. The framework enables multi-step reasoning through language decision processes (LDPs) and has been integrated into FutureHouse's broader AI scientist platform. However, adoption remains limited to research and early commercial contexts, with most real-world scientific breakthroughs still pending validation.
research.barriers: Key barriers include: (1) Limited real-world validation—agents excel on benchmarks but have not yet demonstrated novel scientific discoveries at scale; (2) Reliability and hallucination issues—agents sometimes confuse gene names and details, requiring human oversight; (3) Adoption friction—most scientists lack familiarity with agentic workflows and may distrust AI-generated hypotheses without extensive validation.

candidates.name: Loyal AI Assistance (Fiduciary AI Assistance)
candidates.source_quote: One of the things that came out of the augmented intelligence summit was fiduciary AI assistance. I have been calling them loyal AI assistance. There is a loyal AI system that doesn't have selfish interests and works to advance your goals and interests.
candidates.source_quote_context: Anthony Aguirre's response to the 'eucatastrophe' thought experiment near the end of the podcast
candidates.speaker: Anthony Aguirre
candidates.one_liner: A personal AI system explicitly designed to be loyal to the individual user's goals rather than to platform or advertiser interests, contrasted with current assistants like Siri or Alexa.
candidates.mechanism: The system would know the user deeply enough to assist rather than manipulate, with the user remaining in control. It would have no selfish or third-party interests baked in, functioning more like a fiduciary than a product. Some instances could assist with complex scientific problems while others help navigate everyday information dynamics.
candidates.exists_today: Current voice assistants (Siri, Alexa) and LLM-based assistants exist but are designed around platform interests; the 'fiduciary AI' framing was discussed at an augmented intelligence summit as a conceptual proposal without widespread implementation.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre & Anna Yelizarova | On Worldbuilding.md

research.trl_justification: Fiduciary AI exists primarily as conceptual framework and academic research (published papers, design guidelines). Some prototypes and design methodologies have been developed by research institutions, but no commercial deployment or field testing of full loyal AI assistant systems has been documented. The technology remains in research and early design phases.

key_publications.title: Designing Fiduciary Artificial Intelligence
Fiduciary Principles in AI: Utilizing the Duty of Loyalty
Empowering Consumers with Personal AI Agents: Legal Foundations and Design Considerations

research.state_of_the_art: Fiduciary AI remains a conceptual and legal framework rather than a deployed technology. Academic research has developed design methodologies and six-step procedures for implementing fiduciary principles in AI systems, emphasizing duty of loyalty and care. Current voice assistants (Siri, Alexa) and LLM-based systems continue to prioritize platform and advertiser interests. Recent work explores how existing legal frameworks like UETA could support personal AI agents operating under fiduciary duties, but no commercial systems have been built or deployed at scale with explicit fiduciary obligations to users.
research.barriers: Primary barriers include: (1) Business model misalignment—platforms derive revenue from data monetization and advertising, creating structural conflicts with fiduciary duty to users; (2) Technical challenges in verifying and auditing loyalty at scale, including difficulty measuring whether an AI system is free from third-party influence and consistently prioritizes user goals; (3) Regulatory and legal uncertainty—fiduciary frameworks remain underdeveloped for AI, with no clear enforcement mechanisms or standards for compliance, making companies reluctant to adopt such models without legal clarity.

candidates.name: Windfall Clause
candidates.source_quote: One paper that was interesting out of FHI was the Windfall Clause. This was an agreement where all these companies were building AGI. They agreed beforehand that if they build AI then a certain percentage of their money is reallocated into a trust.
candidates.source_quote_context: Anna Yelizarova's response to the 'eucatastrophe' thought experiment near the end of the podcast
candidates.speaker: Anna Yelizarova (citing FHI paper)
candidates.one_liner: A pre-committed contractual agreement among AGI-developing companies to redirect a percentage of windfall profits into a redistributive trust if they successfully build AGI.
candidates.mechanism: Companies developing AGI would sign on to the clause before achieving AGI, committing a defined share of extraordinary profits to a trust fund. This mechanism is designed to prevent extreme concentration of AGI-generated wealth and ensure broader societal benefit from the technology.
candidates.exists_today: Proposed in a Future of Humanity Institute paper; no major AI companies have formally adopted it, though it has been discussed in AI governance circles.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre & Anna Yelizarova | On Worldbuilding.md

research.trl_justification: Concept-stage policy proposal with theoretical analysis and design frameworks developed, but no real-world implementation, pilot programs, or company commitments. Exists as academic research and governance discussion without operational deployment.

key_publications.title: The Windfall Clause: Distributing the Benefits of AI for the Common Good
The Windfall Clause (AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society)

research.state_of_the_art: The Windfall Clause remains a theoretical policy proposal with no formal adoption by major AI companies. The Future of Life Institute is actively developing implementation frameworks including legal structures, governance models, and distribution mechanisms, with plans to spin out a dedicated non-profit entity as of late 2024. Academic and policy discussions continue in AI governance circles, but the concept has not progressed beyond the design and deliberation phase. No binding commitments or pilot implementations exist among leading AI developers.
research.barriers: Major barriers include uncertainty about legal enforceability and corporate willingness to commit to profit-sharing before achieving windfall status; concerns about whether companies with AGI-level capabilities would honor commitments if enforcement mechanisms become weak; and fundamental questions about how to define windfall thresholds, distribute proceeds, and ensure accountability across jurisdictions. Additionally, no major AI companies have publicly committed to the clause, limiting its practical viability without broader industry coordination.

candidates.name: Large-scale AI-mediated deliberation system
candidates.source_quote: With language models, we have the capability for a thousand people to have a conversation with another thousand people in real time. That's something we've never had the possibility for before, and we can now do it. I don't think we're quite doing it yet, but I suspect we will. What does that look like? That enables us to do things we could never do before—have 100,000 people come to a negotiated agreement on something in a real way.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of what excites the speaker about Tool AI futures, roughly two-thirds through the conversation
candidates.speaker: Anthony (last name not given)
candidates.one_liner: A system using language models to facilitate real-time structured deliberation and negotiated agreement among thousands or hundreds of thousands of people simultaneously.
candidates.mechanism: Language models mediate conversations between large groups of people in real time, aggregating and structuring preferences in ways that crowd dynamics alone cannot. Unlike voting (one bit of information every few years) or online shouting matches, the system would allow genuine back-and-forth negotiation at scale. The speaker envisions it as a tool-based complement to elected representation, not a replacement.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in projects like Polis (used in Taiwan's vTaiwan process) and various AI-assisted deliberation experiments, but nothing operating at the scale or real-time negotiation depth described.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre | Tools or Agents? Choosing Our AI Future.md

key_publications.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation
Can AI Mediation Improve Democratic Deliberation?
Towards Human-AI Deliberation: Design and Evaluation of LLM-Empowered Deliberative AI for AI-Assisted Decision-Making

research.state_of_the_art: Polis enables large-scale opinion mapping with 40,000+ participants and has influenced policy in Taiwan, but operates through discrete statement voting rather than real-time negotiation. The Habermas Machine demonstrates LLMs can mediate group deliberation better than human mediators in controlled experiments with smaller groups. vTaiwan recently integrated generative AI for transcript analysis and opinion clustering. However, no system currently operates at the proposed scale (hundreds of thousands) with real-time back-and-forth negotiation mediated by language models. Most implementations remain asynchronous or semi-synchronous rather than truly real-time.
research.barriers: Technical challenges include maintaining factual accuracy in LLM-generated statements at scale, preventing hallucination, and ensuring fairness in how AI mediators represent diverse perspectives. Governance barriers include establishing democratic legitimacy and accountability for AI-mediated decisions, managing participant knowledge gaps on complex issues, and integrating AI-generated consensus into actual policy-making processes. Scaling challenges involve managing real-time interactions with hundreds of thousands of simultaneous participants while maintaining deliberative quality and preventing manipulation or gaming of the system.

candidates.name: Epistemic stack
candidates.source_quote: There is no reason why, when reading a newspaper article about something, you shouldn't be able to trace back: where did that quote come from, or where did this piece of information come from? How do I know whether to trust this?... We should be able to have a stack we can follow all the way from the high level back down to the raw ingredients, and then figure out how much we trust each of those steps.
candidates.source_quote_context: Answer to the final question about concrete shovel-ready Tool AI ideas, near the end of the conversation
candidates.speaker: Anthony (last name not given)
candidates.one_liner: A citation and provenance system for all information—from newspaper articles to social media claims—that lets users trace any assertion back to its raw data sources, with trust scores based on historical accuracy of each link in the chain.
candidates.mechanism: Every piece of information carries machine-readable provenance metadata linking it to its source, analogous to academic citations but applied universally. AI tools help users traverse this chain from a high-level claim down to raw data, which could be cryptographically signed by hardware secure enclaves and registered on a blockchain. Each node in the chain (person, outlet, inference step) accumulates a reliability record based on past accuracy, allowing users to assess how much to trust any given claim.
candidates.exists_today: Partial implementations exist in academic citation graphs, fact-checking overlays (e.g., Community Notes), and some blockchain-based content provenance projects (e.g., C2PA standard for media). No unified system spans from raw sensor data through inference to published claims with per-node trust scoring.
candidates.source_file: podcast/Anthony Aguirre | Tools or Agents? Choosing Our AI Future.md

Architecting Trust in Artificial Epistemic Agents

research.state_of_the_art: Partial implementations exist across three domains: C2PA Content Credentials provide cryptographically signed provenance metadata for digital media with adoption by camera makers and news outlets; Community Notes on X demonstrates crowdsourced fact-checking at scale with 133,000+ contributors and tens of millions of daily views; academic citation graphs and blockchain-based systems (Numbers Protocol/Capture) add immutability layers. However, no unified system integrates raw sensor data provenance through multi-step inference chains to published claims with per-node historical accuracy scoring. The epistemic stack concept remains largely theoretical, with significant gaps between media provenance (C2PA), claim-level context (Community Notes), and source-level trust metrics.
research.barriers: Technical integration challenges: linking cryptographic provenance from hardware sensors through AI inference steps to final claims requires standardized metadata formats and interoperability across heterogeneous systems. Trust and incentive misalignment: per-node accuracy scoring requires historical ground truth that is expensive to establish and maintain, and platforms have shown reluctance to implement transparent provenance systems (Meta abandoned third-party fact-checkers in 2025). Scalability and adoption: Community Notes shows only 11% of submitted notes reach 'helpful' status, and coverage remains inconsistent; universal adoption would require coordination across competing platforms and jurisdictions with conflicting privacy and regulatory requirements.

candidates.name: Protein-based nanomachines for in vivo tissue repair and cleanup
candidates.source_quote: One of the things that we're very interested in now, which I think was in Eric's talk 20 years ago, is designing nanomachines that can circulate and clean up stuff that shouldn't be there, repair broken tissue, and so forth. And because we can design these new catalytic sites, we can use fuel molecules that nature never thought of. For example, it could be something that's in your diet, like there could be some type of food or food additive that actually when you eat it, it goes into your circulation through your body.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of molecular machines as the next industrial revolution, mid-interview
candidates.speaker: David Baker
candidates.one_liner: Designed protein nanomachines that circulate in the body, powered by dietary fuel molecules, to repair tissue and clear pathological material such as amyloid fibrils.
candidates.mechanism: The machines combine three engineered protein capabilities: target binding, conformational change (to transduce energy into motion), and catalysis (to hydrolyze a fuel molecule). A dietary compound—chosen specifically so it is not ubiquitous in food, allowing on/off control—enters circulation after ingestion and powers the cyclical mechanical action of the protein machine. The machine can then perform tasks such as disaggregating amyloid fibrils or clearing cellular debris outside cells, where no natural quality-control machinery exists.
candidates.exists_today: Baker Lab has prototype machines powered by chemical fuels and by light; natural molecular motors (myosin, kinesin) are well-characterized but not de novo designed. No dietary-fueled, therapeutically functional de novo protein nanomachine has been demonstrated in vivo.
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Baker | Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems.md

key_publications.title: De novo designed rotary proteins
De novo protein design—From new structures to programmable functions

research.state_of_the_art: De novo protein design has achieved significant advances in creating novel protein structures and functions using AI and computational methods. Baker Lab has demonstrated designed rotary protein components and conformational switches that can be controlled with small molecule inputs. Prototype protein nanomachines with rotor and axle components have been assembled in vitro. However, no dietary-fueled, therapeutically functional de novo protein nanomachine has been demonstrated in vivo for tissue repair or amyloid clearance. Current work focuses on designing defined dynamics, conformational changes, and molecular machines as components, but therapeutic in vivo applications remain at early stages.
research.barriers: Major barriers include: (1) achieving reliable in vivo function of designed proteins in the complex biological environment, including circulation, tissue penetration, and avoiding immune clearance; (2) designing and controlling multi-step catalytic cycles powered by dietary fuel molecules while maintaining specificity and avoiding off-target effects; (3) demonstrating that designed nanomachines can perform complex therapeutic tasks like disaggregating amyloid fibrils or clearing cellular debris outside cells where natural quality-control systems do not exist.

candidates.name: De novo designed universal flu vaccines (Neil King / Baker Lab platform)
candidates.source_quote: My colleague Neil King actually made the first de novo design medicine, a vaccine, and he's working to make universal flu vaccines and in general vaccines that could protect against as-yet-unknown viruses.
candidates.source_quote_context: Discussion of health applications of protein design, late in the interview
candidates.speaker: David Baker (describing Neil King's work)
candidates.one_liner: Computationally designed protein nanoparticle scaffolds that present conserved viral epitopes to generate broad, cross-strain protective immunity against influenza and future unknown viruses.
candidates.mechanism: De novo protein design is used to create self-assembling nanoparticle scaffolds that display conserved antigenic regions of influenza (and potentially other viruses) in precise geometric arrangements. Because the scaffold and antigen presentation geometry are designed from first principles rather than derived from attenuated virus, the platform can be rapidly retargeted to novel pathogens. The goal is to elicit antibodies against epitopes shared across many strains, providing universal rather than strain-specific protection.
candidates.exists_today: Neil King's lab has published de novo designed nanoparticle vaccines that entered clinical trials (e.g., ferritin-based and two-component nanoparticle flu vaccine candidates). A fully universal flu vaccine is not yet approved or deployed at scale.

research.state_of_the_art: De novo designed nanoparticle flu vaccines have advanced from preclinical animal studies to Phase 1 human clinical trials. FluMos-v1 began first-in-human testing in 2021 and remains ongoing; FluMos-v2 initiated Phase 1 enrollment in 2025. Preclinical data show the mosaic nanoparticle vaccine provides 92% protection against mismatched strains (H5, H7) compared to 12% for commercial vaccines in animal models. A ferritin-based H2 vaccine completed Phase 1 trials demonstrating safety and cross-reactive antibody responses. The platform has also yielded the first computationally designed COVID-19 vaccine approved in the UK and South Korea, validating the broader approach.
research.barriers: Manufacturing scale-up and standardization remain challenging; particle heterogeneity, improper antigen folding, and antigen interference with nanoparticle assembly must be overcome. Regulatory pathways for universal vaccines are uncertain—approval may require large, expensive efficacy trials demonstrating prevention of illness rather than just correlates of protection, significantly increasing development costs and timelines.

candidates.name: Universal Constructor
candidates.source_quote: I think it will be important, and after the universal constructor is first built, it can then build exponentially more. The human role in production will no longer ever involve unpleasant physical work. Toil will be completely ended by the invention of the universal constructor.
candidates.source_quote_context: Near the end of the podcast, in response to the 'eucatastrophe' question from Beatrice Erkers
candidates.speaker: David Deutsch
candidates.one_liner: A physical machine that can be programmed to construct any physically possible object or perform any physically possible transformation, analogous to a universal computer but for matter.
candidates.mechanism: A universal constructor must be perfectly obedient to its program and capable of being reprogrammed to perform any task not prohibited by the laws of physics. Like a universal computer generalizes computation, a universal constructor generalizes physical fabrication. Deutsch envisions it as something like a computer paired with a robot, where humans provide knowledge and programming rather than physical labor, with sophisticated AI-like interfaces (analogous to ChatGPT for code) handling the translation of intent into constructor instructions.
candidates.exists_today: Constructor theory as a research program exists (developed by Deutsch and Chiara Marletto). Modern CNC machines, 3D printers, and robotic manufacturing are narrow constructors. No general-purpose universal constructor has been built; Deutsch notes 'we do not know how to make a real universal constructor yet.'
candidates.source_file: podcast/David Deutsch | On Beauty, Knowledge, and Progress.md
