key_publications.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Citizens' Assemblies: Benefits, Concerns and Future Pathways
Five dimensions of scaling democratic deliberation: With and beyond AI
Analysing the Global Assembly's influence: The challenges of linking to the deliberative system of global climate governance

research.state_of_the_art: Deliberative mini-publics and citizens' assemblies are well-established globally, with hundreds documented by the OECD. AI integration into deliberative processes is emerging, with tools for sensemaking, translation, and accessibility being prototyped in field pilots (MIT CCC/DemocracyNext, Stanford). Large-scale deliberative processes have been conducted (Global Assembly on Climate with 100 participants; Meta/Stanford deliberative poll with ~6,000 participants), demonstrating feasibility of multilingual, geographically distributed deliberation. However, a standardized, on-demand, globally scalable service model with advance market commitments does not yet exist. The Global Deliberation Coordinator concept was developed in a 2024 hackathon and is being incubated, but remains in early-stage institutional development.
research.barriers: Key barriers include: (1) Ensuring high-quality deliberation across diverse cultural and policy contexts while maintaining representativeness and socioeconomic diversity—previous global assemblies have skewed toward middle- to high-income participants; (2) Establishing institutional linkages and political pathways for deliberative outputs to influence actual policy decisions, as demonstrated by limited impact of the Global Assembly on climate governance; (3) Scaling costs and complexity of multilingual facilitation, secure virtual spaces, and human-quality deliberation at global scale, which may require AI facilitation but raises concerns about bias, transparency, and democratic legitimacy.

candidates.name: Request for Evaluation (RfE) Protocol
candidates.source_quote: Draft Request for Evaluation (RfE) protocol: Outline the requirements for evaluation organizations seeking certification. Develop a certification protocol for AI evaluation organizations that the EU AI Office can use.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on the Evals for Evals Institute, Goals and Next Steps subsections
candidates.speaker: Bogdana Rakova, Kyle Kilian, Maximilian Negele, Nico Miailhe, Siméon Campos, Tilman Räuker
candidates.one_liner: A certification protocol that evaluates and certifies the organizations conducting AI safety evaluations, rather than evaluating AI systems directly.
candidates.mechanism: The RfE protocol defines requirements that evaluation organizations must meet to receive certification, analogous to how labs are accredited. It harmonizes diverse assessment methods into a structured field while preventing 'safety washing' from poorly designed evaluations. The protocol is designed to align with EU AI Office standards and is developed through stakeholder input from industry and academia before being submitted to the European Commission for implementation.
candidates.exists_today: AI evaluation frameworks exist (e.g., NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act conformity assessments), but a meta-level certification protocol specifically for the organizations conducting frontier AI pre-deployment evals does not exist.
candidates.source_file: x-hope/hackaton-report.md

research.trl_justification: No evidence of this specific protocol existing in development or deployment. Related frameworks exist but do not match the described RfE Protocol mechanism.
research.state_of_the_art: While the EU AI Act establishes conformity assessment requirements for high-risk AI systems and the EU AI Office is developing evaluation methodologies and standards, no published meta-level certification protocol specifically for frontier AI evaluation organizations exists. Related work includes ISO/IEC 42001 for organizational AI governance, IEEE CertifAIEd™ for AI ethics, and NIST frameworks, but these target AI systems or organizational practices rather than certifying evaluation organizations themselves.
research.barriers: The concept of certifying evaluation organizations as a distinct institutional layer is nascent and faces challenges including: (1) lack of consensus on what constitutes adequate evaluation standards for frontier AI systems, (2) tension between standardization and methodological diversity in evaluation approaches, and (3) unclear governance authority for implementing such a protocol across jurisdictions.

candidates.name: World Convention on Transformative Artificial Intelligence (WCTAI)
candidates.source_quote: Development of a roadmap to the WCTAI, with stakeholder precommitments of engagement when certain technological trigger conditions recognizing TAI development are met. Conduct preparatory research, including research to define the milestones signaling TAI development, to ensure inclusive representation and deliberation processes, and to evaluate potential global governance options.
candidates.source_quote_context: Section on the World Convention on Transformative Artificial Intelligence, Success Metrics and Next Steps subsections
candidates.speaker: Brandon Goldman, Fin Moorhouse, José Villalobos, Ludwig Illies, Saad Siddiqui, Stephen Clare
candidates.one_liner: A pre-negotiated global convention on TAI governance that is automatically triggered when predefined technological development milestones are reached.
candidates.mechanism: Stakeholders pre-commit to engaging in the convention when specific, research-defined TAI development milestones are met, creating a conditional activation mechanism. Preparatory diplomatic work and research on governance models, deliberative formats, and milestone definitions are conducted in advance so the convention can convene rapidly once triggered. Draft agreements for state signatories are prepared beforehand to accelerate the process.
candidates.exists_today: International AI governance summits exist (e.g., UK AI Safety Summit), but a pre-committed, milestone-triggered global convention with pre-negotiated stakeholder commitments and pre-drafted agreements does not.
candidates.source_file: x-hope/hackaton-report.md

key_publications.title: A Global Convention for the Intelligence Explosion
Global AI Regulation at a Time of Transformation: The Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence

research.state_of_the_art: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (adopted May 2024, opened for signature September 2024) is the world's first binding international AI treaty, covering AI systems across their lifecycle with focus on human rights, democracy, and rule of law. However, it is not milestone-triggered and lacks pre-negotiated activation mechanisms. Conceptual research on threshold-triggered global conventions exists but remains theoretical. Current international AI governance relies on non-binding declarations (Bletchley, Seoul, Hiroshima AI Process) and regional legislation (EU AI Act). No pre-committed, milestone-triggered convention with pre-drafted agreements has been negotiated or implemented.
research.barriers: Major barriers include: (1) Geopolitical fragmentation—key AI actors like China and Russia are absent from existing treaties, limiting global reach and enforcement; (2) Technical challenge of defining objective, verifiable TAI development milestones that would trigger automatic convention activation without gaming or dispute; (3) Political feasibility—states resist pre-committing to binding obligations triggered by external events, preferring negotiation at the time of activation.
